utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We shall continue with the examination-in-chief of Mr. Bogosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bogosavljevic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The examination by Mr. Ivetic will continue. I have to remind you that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to your evidence today. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning again, Mr. Bogosavljevic. I'd like to try and pick up where we left off yesterday. Yesterday, I believe you had been talking about your own police officers, saying that their authority was limited to the trains, and I have a question for you with respect to the other organs of the interior, other police officers, from the various -- that had the responsibility for the various trains stations. Did you ever see or did any of your police officers ever report that those police at the train stations were involved in mistreating or robbing people?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were policemen at every train station from that area; however, I have no knowledge of those policemen being involved in any acts of forcing passengers to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the record, can the interpreters hear me on this microphone because I've been getting lots of feedback on this one so I decided to change. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask you for a moment -- we already handled Pec, I think, so that question is done. I'd like to ask you about Kosovo Polje briefly. First of all, as being someone who spent an awful lot of time in the town or city of Kosovo Polje during 1998 and 1999, I'd like to ask you to comment upon some testimony we had here in this case from other persons. We've had some evidence from the one witness at least who said that his source came from Bosnia that a paramilitary group, the Wolves of the Drina led by Commander Karasek, were based in Kosovo Polje. Can you agree with that assertion based upon the size of Kosovo Polje and your knowledge of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a foundational objection. I don't know that we've heard about the size of Kosovo Polje yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's correct were Mr. Hannis. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, that's correct. Why don't I do it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, as someone who spent a lot of time in Kosovo Polje in 1998 and 1999, was -- size-wise, would you consider it likely or even possible for strange faces to appear and not be noticed by the locals?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't possible. Kosovo Polje at the time had 4 or 5.000 inhabitants, and they all knew each other more or less. Every new unit that would arrive was noticed and people would know where those people would be stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now I'd like to ask you, again, to comment on the evidence that we've had from one witness who said that a paramilitary group from Bosnia, the Wolves of the Drina led by a Commander Legenda Karasek, were based in Kosovo Polje. Can you comment on that assertion based on your knowledge of Kosovo Polje during the relevant time-period?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of such a unit in the area of Kosovo Polje. What I do know is that the SAJ had a base in Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This may seem redundant, but we've also had evidence that a paramilitary group belonging to Arkan was based in Kosovo Polje, and, likewise, that the JSO was headquartered in Kosovo Polje. Based upon your same knowledge of Kosovo Polje, would you comment on the likelihood of that.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can repeat that I only know of the SAJ having a base in Kosovo Polje. Apart from VJ, there were no other units in the area of Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, we've also had evidence in this case that at the train station in Pristina, from the 25th of March for a period of three days, civilians were kept there and that the -- one witness, Emin Kabashi, in his statement said that there were approximately twelve trains daily for Macedonia. Do you have any knowledge with which you could add to this -- to our understanding of the situation in the -- with the trains departing from Pristina for Macedonia during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the air-strikes, meaning the 24th of March, and during the following four to five days, there was not a single train that left Pristina or Kosovo Polje for Macedonia; therefore, that witness's statement is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, we had another witness, Nazlie Bala, in her sworn statement, that's P2262 on the fourth page, she claimed that she saw trains with as many as 30 passenger -- passenger cars or wagons, as I think they're called in Serbian. Could you comment upon that based upon your knowledge and work experience. Is such a thing possible during the time-period 1999 when you were commander of the Kosovo Polje station?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state that not a single train or engine we had at our disposal at the moment could pull as many as 30 cars. We had very poor vehicles at our disposal at the time because of the terrain toward Djeneral Jankovic and Macedonia. There is the Kacanik gorge there and it's very steep. We didn't have a single engine that could pull 30 cars. In most cases, it would be ten, 12, up to 15 cars at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, what could you tell us about NATO bombing of railway lines either heading towards Serbia or towards the other directions?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the air-strikes, I don't remember the exact date, but a tunnel between Pristina and Kursumlija was bombed as well as a railway bridge just past Zvecani in the direction of Kraljevo. Therefore, our communication in that regard with Serbia was interrupted. As for the direction towards Macedonia, there were no interruptions in terms of railway traffic at all. However, as of the 24th and in the next four to five days, there were not enough train captains at our disposal, and that is why there were no trains leaving Kosovo Polje during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bogosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have completed my questioning for this witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. It may be we've had evidence about this before but I just don't remember it. The railway line at Kosovo Polje is a station that the train can go through obviously. Do trains from Pristina to Macedonia go through Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why is Kosovo Polje the bigger station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kosovo Polje is the starting point for all directions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you're travelling from Pristina to Macedonia, do you have to change trains at Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bogosavljevic, good morning. My name is Djuro Cepic, attorney-at-law, appearing on behalf of General Lazarevic. Can you tell me whether army members provided security to the train stations in Pristina and Kosovo Polje, as well as any other train stations in the area of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not notice any army members at any train station, save for Djeneral Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were army members providing security in terms of railway lines and directions within the area of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bogosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bogosavljevic. If I understood your testimony correctly, from 1971 to 1986, you were working as a traffic policeman?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then, from 1986 until 1992, you were an inspector doing on-site investigations of traffic accidents, right?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did you do in Serbia between 1999 and your retirement in 2005? What was your job there?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was -- I was the head of the rolling stock at the gendarmerie headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you hold any rank or title at the time of your retirement?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My rank was that of a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you don't mind, I'll call you captain because it's easier for me than trying to pronounce your name, I have a hard time. Captain, you said you were appointed commander of the police station for railway security in Kosovo Polje in 1992. What were your exact duties? What did you do every day when you went to your job? Can you give us a brief description of that.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My daily duties were making up the roster and planning patrols which were supposed to go on different trains.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your hours, what hours did you work? Did you work a day shift?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what period exactly you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Fair enough. I want to focus on late 1998 and the first half of 1999, including during the war, during the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My work hours were approximately 14, 15 hours in any 24-hour day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you working seven days a week?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I resided in Kosovo Polje. The station was nearby, and I would walk to work every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So you went -- you didn't have weekends off. You worked seven days a week; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would go there occasionally. Perhaps, during the course of any weekend, I'd be there for an hour or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You told us yesterday, I think, that although you were supposed to have I think 66 people, you only had a total of 37 working for you, is that right, in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who did you report to? I think you told us you reported to the SUP, but who -- was there a particular individual whose name you can tell us that was your superior that you reported to?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say I reported to the SUP but to the head of the police department within the Pristina SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell me his name?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zarko Brakovic or his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the deputy's name?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vesko Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You and your men and women wore, what, these standard blue police uniform, or was there a standard uniform for the railway security?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until May 1998, we wore standard blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from then until June 1999, what uniforms did you wear?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that point on until June 1999, we wore blue camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during that period from May 1998 to June 1999, what kind of weapons, if any, did you and your people carry?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to interject, but so far every single question is one that we've had in direct examination yesterday, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know some of this was covered, but I don't know if we were specific about time-periods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was specific. The uniforms I remember clearly being --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the prior, about the superiors he reported to, that was all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And, certainly, the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have no problem with him asking it again; it's just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's his loss in the end of the day --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Mr. Ivetic, but it's sometimes helpful just to remind us that we need to concentrate on what really matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is my loss.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you answer that question for me, though, between May 1998 and June 1999, what kind of weapons did you and your people carry?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Side-arms and rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic asked you yesterday if any entity called the MUP staff or the staff of the ministry had any effect on your role or your work; and you said, no, except for the police department and the Pristina SUP. Did you ever hear of a body called the Ministry Staff for the Suppression of Terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija? Did you ever hear that term in 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the term the Ministry Staff for the Suppression of Terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija? Did you ever hear of that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of the MUP staff; however, I don't know of any staff for the suppression of terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned how you were appointed to your position as the commander on the recommendation of the Pristina SUP chief. Who was the chief that appointed you or recommended your appointment?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, it was Bosko Petric.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The position you held, were there other similar jobs like that in Kosovo, or was yours in Kosovo Polje the only position? Were there other commanders of railway security offices in other locations in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were none. Ours was the only station in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, by that, do I take it that you and your 37 people were the entire contingent of the police responsible for railway security on the trains in movement in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And those 37 police officers, what hours did they work? Did they work eight-hour shifts or 12-hour shifts and how many days a week in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A patrol would board the train and stay with it until its destination. The working hours depended on the schedule. On occasion, it could have been as short as four hours, and then the same patrol could escort another train for, say, another six hours. So ten to 12 hours a day, a single patrol would cover several trains moving in different directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how many days a week would your people work without having a day off? Did they work seven days a week or did they have days off?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had one day a week off.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And how many -- during an average weekday, how many trains would be running in Kosovo? You told us about the different lines that you serviced, but how many trains on average would go a day, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the day, on average, there were ten to 12 trains.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And your typical patrol would be two persons per train, right?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned - I don't want you to mention the names now - but you mentioned in private session three people that were working for you. Did those people work for you throughout the war? Did they stay the whole time? I don't remember if you told us.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They stayed until some point towards the middle of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then what happened? Did they leave?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since pressure was exerted against their families, they left the service and they left Kosovo and Metohija together with their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What were their specific jobs? Were those three also regular police people, or did they have some other kind of job?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were also policemen and they also went out on patrols together with the other policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. For somebody travelling from Pristina to Djeneral Jankovic, we've had some evidence about people boarding the train in Pristina. I think Judge Bonomy just asked you if the person boarding in Pristina then would have to change in Kosovo Polje, and your answer was yes. Was that true during the war as well?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It only applied to regular traffic before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And, during the war, we've had evidence about a number of trains going from Pristina to Djeneral Jankovic, and I believe the evidence was that they went from Pristina straight to Djeneral Jankovic without stopping in Kosovo Polje on -- sometimes without stopping in Urosevac. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the fact that there were a few trains that were going from Pristina to Djeneral Jankovic, but I claim that they all had to stop in Kosovo Polje and Urosevac at the railway stations there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you wouldn't be in a position to know whether or not they stopped in Urosevac, right, because you weren't there? And I'm talking particularly about the time-period between the 29th of March and the 15th of April. You were never in Urosevac during that time-period to see whether the trains stopped there, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in Urosevac, but I was on the train a few times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us when you were on the train between the 29th of March and the 15th of April, 1999? First of all, can you tell us how many times?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, twice, but I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you remember anything else about those two times. Was it just a regular train, or was it a special train with additional cars? Who was travelling? Anything you can tell us about those two occasions?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were regular trains with about ten cars full of passengers, predominantly Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, on those two occasions, did you ride to the end of the line in Djeneral Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to yourself and the passengers, were there other police or soldiers on the train?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My police patrol was there and there were the passengers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And no soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you didn't see what happened to the passengers after they got off the train in Djeneral Jankovic? Did you see them walking along the railroad track toward the border?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them walking down the railroad track towards the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you see any police or VJ directing them in that direction?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw members of the Army of Yugoslavia, but I don't know whether they were directing them or what they were saying to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, we have evidence from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've obviously misunderstood yesterday. Did you always have to get off the train at Djeneral Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police would usually get off the train.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but why did the passengers get off? Did they have to walk through the border and then be picked up again by the train or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Hannis, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My questions were limited to 29th of March to the 15th of April, and he was talking about two occasions when he travelled on the train.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right. So were there no trains at that time going to Macedonia? Sorry, just forget that question. I'll let Mr. Hannis continue about this, but I'm unclear about the circumstances prevailing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We've had evidence from a witness who worked at the train station in Urosevac, that between the beginning of the bombing, on the 24th of March, for about four or five days no trains ran, and I think that's what you said earlier. That's correct, isn't it, that the train traffic stopped for a few days at the beginning of the bombing, right?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that witness also told us that, before the bombing had started, that the general schedule for trains travelling from Kosovo Polje to the Macedonian border ran three times a day in both directions. Three trains would come south heading to Macedonia and three trains would be going north back to Kosovo Polje, so six trains passing through Urosevac on a day. Is that consistent with your knowledge and information about the train schedules in 1999 before the bombing started?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were four trains in one direction and four in the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We also heard evidence that when the trains started running again, after the 29th of March, there were a few days at the very end of March and the beginning of April in which there were more than the usual number of trains, and those trains carried more than the usual number of cars. Were you aware of that? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were these special trains, as railway people call them, one or two a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have enough staff to put people on those additional trains that were running then?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had enough staff because the lines towards Pec and Kursumlija had been stopped. No trains ran on account of the fact that the railroad had been damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during that time, between the 29th of March and the 15th of April, did you have your people put on each and every train going south to the Macedonian border, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, my people were on the train.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you see or did your people tell you that there were thousands of people on these trains during that two-week period going from Pristina to the Macedonian border, standing room only in those trains, right?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that statement, that there were thousands there. One car can have 80 passengers sitting there an additional 20 or 30 can be standing there. Ten cars would take it to a thousand people on one train, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you said, in an answer earlier today, that an engine might carry up to 12 or 15 cars, right?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, but I didn't say that every engine carried 12 to 15 cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And isn't it the practice that sometimes, in the railway business, an extra engine will be coupled to another one so that two engines can pull additional cars? Was that ever done?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you mean as far as you know. You didn't see each and every train that went through your station, right?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I managed to see almost all of them off from Kosovo Polje or to meet them there when they would come back to the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us about filing urgent daily and periodic reports to the police department in the Pristina SUP. Do you have any of those documents?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of information would go in your daily report?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information about the possible forcible stopping of trains, stalling of trains, other breakdowns of law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you note when special trains were passing through or when trains with additional cars passed through, or was that information that did not go into your reports?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because it is the railway administration that decides on special trains and additional cars, whether they will add more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that from your answers yesterday, but that's not something that you would take note of in your report, that's not the kind of information that you would be telling your boss about, right?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during this two-week-plus time-period, between the 29th of March and the 15th of April, you didn't notice any of those trains heading south containing additional police, other than your security police, or soldiers riding along with those passengers who were heading toward Macedonia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, but my patrols were reinforced. There were days when four policemen, even up to six, would go out when there were 12 to 15 cars on a particular train.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You told us that at the beginning of the NATO bombing, you relocated from your police station in one of the buildings belonging to the railway company to a private home in Kosovo Polje. Whose private home did you move to? Was that one that belonged to a fellow employee?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that an abandoned Kosovo Albanian home?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who located there, just you or all 37 of you? Who stayed there?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there with ten of my people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to show you for just a moment Exhibit P3119. This is a map that will come up on your screen in just a minute, and it shows an area between Pristina and Urosevac. I want to ask you about the railway lines and where you were located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bogosavljevic, the ten people you referred to, were they administrative workers or were they policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was one administrative worker and the rest were policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have the map yet on your screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a problem. I don't have it on mine. I don't know if Your Honours have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Looks like the witness does.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the Judges to see it, can you tell me does that generally show accurately where the railroad line ran between Pristina, Kosovo Polje, and Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I see that between Kosovo Polje and Ferizaj, the train also passes through Lipljan. Was there a train station there?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have a hard copy of this? Can we have it on the ELMO, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, captain, we're going to put this on the ELMO because lawyers on the other side aren't able to see it, nor are the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go up just a little bit to try and -- well, that will do for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On this map, can you indicate for us approximately where your offices were located before the bombing started? And there's a pen you can use to draw a circle.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you direct the witness, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Captain, could you -- on this map, are you able to draw a circle or an "X" indicating approximately where your offices were located in Kosovo Polje before the coming started?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For everyone to see it, it will have to be drawn on the map on the ELMO, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if you can just then point on the map that's on the ELMO to your left, sir. With the help of the usher standing next to you, if you could just use a pointer to indicate on that map.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I see you've indicated a mark between the "F" in Fushe Kosove and Kosovo Polje. Thank you. And when you moved after the bombing started, can you indicate that second location?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I see you put a second mark just to the right of that between "U" in Fushe and the "O" in Kosovo below it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know how we can handle that. I don't know if I can give that an IC number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It can be given an IC number and then scanned later, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we may do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC190, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. I don't need anything further from that at the moment, unless Your Honours have a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us, yesterday, sir, that regarding any complaints about theft from civilians on the trains that: "During 1999, I can state that not a single crime was reported to me or any of my policemen." How does that compare with the number of crimes reported to you in 1998? Do you recall getting any crime reports in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the actual figure. There probably was some theft but very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would it have been more than ten?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's usually petty theft, pick-pocketing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You told us that as far as the number of trains and whether special trains will run, et cetera, it's something that falls under the railway administration. What ministry is the railway administration under, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The railways of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during a state of war, do you know what happens then under the law. Does -- do the decisions about running the railroad continue to fall under the railway administration, or does it go to the army or some other body, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was decided by the railway administration only.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What is the extent of your knowledge about that? Did someone tell you that, did you see it written down somewhere, or are you just guessing?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not go into this particular subject matter, but I know that it wasn't the police that could decide about that, I assume, or the army for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like they couldn't interfere in our affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said, "Concerning the arrival," and this is page 29 from yesterday. "Concerning the arrivals of special or previously not scheduled trains to Kosovo Polje, that's something I have never been advised of." Does that mean you wouldn't receive advanced notice when special trains were going to be running?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would receive notice about special trains so that I could prepare a patrol for such a train.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how far in advance would you typically receive such notice?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually, today for a train, that would be running tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During the time-period between 29 March and 15 April, we have evidence from a document and from a witness named Bajram Bucaliu, who worked in Urosevac, that there were a number of special trains running during that time-period. Did you receive advanced notice for all those special trains, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, unless he's going to show the document, I don't know how any witness can answer whether they received advanced notice for all those special trains without knowing which those are and the numbers, the dates, et cetera. I mean, it's a very unfair question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On the list of exhibits that I was provided that might be used with you was Exhibit P1331, which is the log-book from the Urosevac train station. Were you shown that document during your preparation to testify here?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall looking at entries for the dates in late March and the first half of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a lot of entries, so I don't know whether I saw those in particular and whether I would be able to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall seeing on a few of those days during that time-period that there were a larger number of trains than normal running on the 31st of March, the 1st and 2nd of April? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were two or three trains in addition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you, yourself, didn't keep any written records at the time of the number of special trains that ran during that time-period, did you? That wasn't your job?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a roster of service for my men; so in that roster, it was planned. The movement of these extra trains was also planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't have a copy of those rosters that you created during that time-period, do you?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us about a problem on the route between Kosovo Polje and Pec; and at page 31, line 4 yesterday you said: "As of May, the train moved without police escort." Were you referring to May 1998 when your police stopped travelling on the Pec-Kosovo Polje route?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did anyone warn passengers travelling on that route that there was no longer going to be a police escort?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Kosovo Polje towards Pec, at that time, there were no passengers; but on the stops along the road - and that's a distance of some 80 kilometres - on stops along the way, passengers came in and stepped off. Those places along the way are mostly populated by Albanians, so the train practically served only them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned today that Kosovo Polje had about 4 or 5.000 inhabitants and they all knew each other more or less, and every new unit that would arrive was noticed and people would know where those people would be stationed. So can you tell me, between 1st of January, 1999 and April of 1999, how many new units arrived in Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I suppose there were no other units apart from the SAJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where was the SAJ unit located, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the centre of Kosovo Polje at the crossroads between Pristina and Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander was?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know approximately when they first came there?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you looked at the train log from Urosevac, Exhibit P1331, were you able to understand the entries? The reason I asked that question is that a witness explained to us that the numbers listed for the trains helped identify in which direction they were travelling. Were you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, I know. You mean directions of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess if we could just take one quick look at a page from that exhibit, it's P1331, and I just want to put up the B/C/S, Your Honour. I think, for purposes of my question, that's all we need. It would be, I believe, it's e-court page number 114.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see the cover of that document. Is that the one you looked at? And now we're at a page where I think the first three entries at the top of the page relate to the 1st of April. I don't know if you can read that, but can you see, in the very top left, that appears to be a 01.04, which the witness before told us was the 1st of April. Would you agree with me about that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it's written, the 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then, so the fourth entry appears to be for the 2nd of April, and I think we -- you can agree with me by looking at the time in column number 5 and 6, which the prior witness explained to us is the time that the train left Urosevac station. You'll see that, in item number 3, the hour was 2325, which I take to mean it was 11.25, just before midnight, on the 1st; and this item number 4 is 225, which I take to mean 2.25 in the morning on April 2nd. Would you agree with that, or have any reason to disagree?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He also explained to us that the southbound trains from Urosevac were identified with an odd number; whereas, those going northbound had an even number. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So by my count on this page for April 2nd, starting at 2.25 in the morning, and going to the bottom of the page where we see an entry for 2215 hours, the number of odd-numbered or southbound-going trains I see are seven. Do you come up with that same number?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall seven trains heading toward the Macedonian border on one day?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably, yes, because on the regular service, there were four trains.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he also explained to us that in column 3, 3:00 and 4:00 is supposed to be the time that the train arrived in the Urosevac station, but you'll see several of these entries just have an arrow or a diagonal mark going from the lower left to the upper right-hand corner of those two blocks. He explained that meant that the train didn't stop, that it passed directly through the station. Were you aware that during this time-period some of those trains continued straight on to the border, apparently without stopping in Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I believe earlier or Mr. Hannis himself objected that this witness would not have knowledge of Urosevac, except for the time that the periods --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, all we're doing is looking at the interpretation of the document at the moment. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you need me to repeat that question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this document of theirs, why the time of stopping is not written, whether this line here is correct, meaning that the train did not stop, because every train had to be stopped at these stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I suggest to you that the reason is that this was during the early weeks of the war and that there were large numbers of Kosovo Albanians being transported to the border so that they could leave the country, and there was no need to stop, right?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was necessary for people to board the train in Urosevac, if they were waiting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But some witnesses have told us some of these trains travelling from Pristina were already jam-packed, and they were crowded in like sardines. Didn't you see that in Kosovo Polje at the end of March and the beginning of April 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they could tell any story they like, but that they were hanging out the windows and out the doors and that they were unable to breathe is not correct, is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say they said that. Did you hear that somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read some statements where that is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Ivetic, re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it will be very brief, Your Honour. While we have this document on the screen, since Mr. Hannis was able to use this and interpret this document, I would like the full picture of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He was cross-examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So please bear in mind that the nature of the questions will be different depending on the role that the examiner is playing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. I understand that as well, Your Honour. And, actually, I don't think I even need to ask the witness this question; but at page 114 of the B/C/S, for the entry of the 2nd of April on the first and second lines, if those lines -- pardon me, the column that has the lines also shows lines for trains going in the opposite direction, going away from the border. So, whatever those lines mean, I'm not going to suggest at this point in time, but I'm just pointing out that Mr. Hannis selectively chose the half story.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, a question that I do have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, that sort of comment in this context simply runs the risk of undermining the strength of any answer the witness might give.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But I didn't does the witness about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All I'm saying to you is that you run that risk, and it's not the appropriate stage for making these submissions anyway. It can be made at the right time. Now, please ask questions. I thought by now I wouldn't have to direct you as to what your job was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogosavljevic, we had some discussion regarding the railway service and the conductors. Could you tell me based upon your knowledge and information what types of uniforms the employees of the railway service utilised in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blue uniforms, darker blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bogosavljevic for your time and your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have no more re-direct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bogosavljevic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to give evidence to the Tribunal and to assist us. You're now free to leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, our next witness is Mr. Bozidar Filic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could with your leave indicate that appearing -- well, present with me in court is Mr. Michael Edwards, who will be assisting and has assisted very much in the preparation of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Filic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document that the usher will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Filic.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you should adjust your headset, lest it falls off.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we lower the ELMO so I can see the witness, please. Can we lower the ELMO so I can see the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we begin?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To begin with, please introduce yourself briefly?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: My name is Bozidar Filic. I was born on the 10th of August, 1954, in Kriljevo village, Kosovska Kamenica municipality, autonomous province Kosovo and Metohija, father's name Trajko, mother's name Savka. I'm married with three children, I currently live in Belgrade as a retired MUP officer, and my status is that of a temporarily displaced person from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about your work history?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: After primary school, I completed the secondary school of internal affairs in Sremska Kamenica. In 1973, after working as a policeman, for a short while, I completed the academy of ground forces. From 1978 to 1982, I worked as deputy commanding officer of the police station in Prizren, when I was transferred in 1982 to the SUP of the province, where I worked as an inspector in the police administration. From end 1982 until 1986, I was deputy commander of the police detachment of the provincial secretariat. Until 1988, I was chief commander of the police detachment; and after that, I worked in the centre of security of the SUP of Pristina. After that, I worked for a while in the staff of the police; and when the PJP was established in 1994, I was commander of the police detachment which was made up from secretariats from Kosovo -- sorry, that was until 1994. Then I was named chief of the SUP of Pristina, deputy chief of the SUP of Pristina, until 15 April 1990, when I was appointed chief of the Urosevac SUP, and I stayed in that position until 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, that's not -- Ah, yes, it is the information I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, date at line 18 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on the record that you were deputy chief of Pristina SUP until the 15th of April, 1990 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Filic, one of the jobs you said you held was, if I can find it again, yes, deputy commander of the police detachment of the provincial secretariat. What is the provincial secretariat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means the secretariat of the province. It was at the time a state authority, the secretariat of interior of the province.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did that exist in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that starting from 15 April 1999, you were chief of Pristina SUP and you were -- stayed there until 2006?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: No, it was Urosevac SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you stayed there until you retired?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were your offices after the 20th of June, 1999?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: After we withdrew from Kosovo and Metohija, SUP Urosevac was located in Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us - and Judge Bonomy also wanted to know about this - that you worked in the provincial SUP?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, at that time, who were the leading people of the provincial SUP?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: At that time, the provincial SUP had within its framework the office of the secretary of that provincial secretariat, deputy secretary, under-secretary for public security, and under-secretary for state security, and a certain number of assistant secretaries. Also, in various lines of work, there were several administrations. Shall I name them?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: Administration for police affairs and traffic safety; administration of crime police; administration for the border and foreign nationals, with a certain number of police units for border crossings, meaning Vrbnica and Cafa Prusit and the one at the airport; administration for communications; administration for information and analysis; administration for common affairs; administration for fire brigade; and the administration for the duty service of the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the detachment?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: There was a police detachment as an organizational unit of the SUP with three units: The special unit for anti-terrorist actions, the unit for the security of installations and persons, and the unit for escorting trains.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many personnel did you have?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: Within this structure, there were about 1.000 employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Filic. I think it's time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Filic, we have to break at this stage as we do each day. Could you please leave the courtroom with the usher while we have the break and we'll see you in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us who the head of the provincial SUP was and you described its composition and administrations. Did the provincial SUP also comprise the secretariat of internal affairs in the field?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: Yes, however, that was towards the end of its existence. In 1997/1998 there was a reorganization.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's where the security centres were introduced?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1988.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's when the centres were created from the then-secretariats of internal affairs which were under the competence of municipalities. Once the security centres were established, they were directly -- they came directly under the provincial SUP in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many centres were there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: Seven security centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does that correspond to the SUPs as they existed in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many people were there in the field in those centres?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly, but more or less the same number as it is nowadays, the number of policemen in the current secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Around 10.000?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please observe a pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, was the provincial SUP issuing orders to the security centres?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the security centres which are equivalent to the current SUPs oblige to report to the provincial SUP?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: They were supposed to report to them the way they nowadays report to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the provincial SUP approving work-plans of the centres -- security centres in the field?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the provincial SUP monitoring the work of the SUPs in Kosovo and Metohija along professional lines?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1999, was the Ministry of Internal Affairs in Belgrade busy doing everything we've been mentioning so far?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we would kindly ask to go briefly into private session in order to protect the identity of some Albanians, so that their names not be known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the basis for saying they may be at risk?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I say so, it could be identified of why I'm asking this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it because of where they now are?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They mostly live in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, what's your position on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure if a basis has been laid, but I think counsel is saying there is some risk so I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in the past, we've been able to unravel this should it be inappropriate, so we'll go into private session for -- out of an abundance of caution.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Filic, did anyone on the Serbian side force those Albanians to leave the service?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: No, no one did. They were even trying to persuade them to stay with the secretariat and the security centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was your position at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: I was chief of the police sector, as it was called then, within the security centre in Pristina. I was in charge of a group of police inspectors within that sector. We oversaw the work of the police in the entire security centre, which is something that falls within the domain of the current police chief or the chief of the police department.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you mention that you were a member of a commission which dealt with this issue?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: When some Albanian superiors decided to leave the then-provincial SUP, the under-secretary for personnel, assistant secretary for personnel, rather, Slobodan Mijovic, established a commission so that those people could leave the service according to the procedure. I was a member of that commission which also comprised Savo Majstorovic, inspector, as well as a chief of the then-department of the SUP, Mr. Kurtesi, who is Gorani. We needed to discharge Seremet Mehmeti who was the then-chief of the police administration within the provincial SUP; and Mr. Trstena, who was head of one of the departments within the police service; and Hajnura Tutava [phoen], who was an inspector with the police administration. We acted accordingly to -- according to the decision of the assistant minister. We tried to talk to them about their reasons for leaving, and they said we had already explained that, there is no explaining it further. We discharged them and there were no objections to the procedure implemented by the commission, save for Mr. Trstena who asked that there should be an Albanian in the commission, since Mr. Bujupi, or rather, Mr. Kurtesi was a Gorani. I advised Under-Secretary Mijovic of that. We tried to find an Albanian to participate in the work of the commission, but they wouldn't. Most of them said, "Well, I wasn't the one who employed him, I'm not going to be one of those discharges him." I passed that information to the assistant secretary, and that was the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you take in new policemen?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: Given that a great many policemen left the force, we needed to take on new people, and we also needed to temporarily dispatch certain police forces from Serbia proper. Since the security situation was ever-changing and it was unstable, we couldn't preserve the security situation with the number of people we were left with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you had tenders for new people to be taken on board?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: The ministry did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were the same conditions provided for employment to both Serbs and Albanians?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The policemen who had previously left the service, could they also apply?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: They could; but as far as I know, none of them tried to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how long did the training of those new policemen last?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: It was organized in Vucitrn, Novi Sad, and Belgrade. It lasted for a year with six months of theoretical curriculum and six months of practical work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the relationship between the ethnic communities in Kosovo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: The inter-ethnic relations in Kosovo in 1998, in my assessment and the assessment of the service, was very complicated. The leaders of the Albanian people, by using gatherings of different types, were trying to organize and line up their population. I wanted to mention the issue of the infamous poisoning of members of a single ethnic community in Vucitrn --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In Podujevo

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- which caused great resentment among the Albanians in Kosovo. There was also another gathering, as they called it, the burial of violence which gathered tens of thousands of Albanians. They were moving along the streets of Pristina with an empty coffin, taking the coffin to a Muslim cemetery, symbolically trying to bury the Serbian violence against their population. This also caused a wave of moving out and away from the region among many Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that there was a poisoning of members of a single ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: In elementary school in Podujevo, allegedly, there was a case of poisoning of only Albanian children, whereas, in fact, in the same class, there were children of other ethnicities as well. They made a scene, basically. There were paramedics and a lot of attention. It wasn't possible for Albanian children to be poisoned alone without Serbian and R omani children suffering the same fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any terrorist attacks in -- in the 1990s, before 1998, in the area of the Pristina SUP?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: There were terrorist attacks, especially in the area of Podujevo and Glogovac OUPs. A number, a great number of terrorist attacks was carried out, a number of our employees were killed. In Podujevo, for example, an inspector was killed. He was from the crime police, his name was Milos Stojanovic, and he was accompanied by a reserve policeman, Rakic. They were riddled with bullets in the vehicle they were in, in front of one of their houses. In Glogovac, there was the case of the 13th of May, 1993, when there was a terrorist attack on a van transporting employees of the Pristina SUP Glogovac OUP. The van was taking them to work. They were ambushed at a railroad crossing in Glogovac. Several of them were killed, several wounded. Later on, during the proceedings, it was established that Hashim Thaqi executed that attack, together with his group.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we're going to move on to 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Filic, it may be that you could assist the interpreters by speaking perhaps a little more slowly, especially when you're giving quite a long answer. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1998, were you the spokesperson of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: I was the spokesperson of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia from June 1998 until the beginning of the aggression, the 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Along parallel lines, did you have another duty; and if so, which one?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: The deputy chief of the SUP of Pristina, so I carried out this other duty along parallel lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who appointed you spokesperson?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: The chief of SUP of Pristina informed me that the minister decided that the collegium of the ministry decided, in the forthcoming period, I would be the spokesperson in order to help foreign journalists to get the right kind of information about Kosovo, because I was from the area and I was very familiar with the entire province.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to show you 5D1239; and, first, we should have a look at some footage from Malisevo. You're not here, but I'm going to ask you something in relation to this once you've seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, was this to be translated for us because it's not happening for me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is impossible to interpret without a transcript. This is very fast and the sound quality is poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the witness can explain, and I think that the reporter is speaking so fast that it would be impossible to provide simultaneous interpretation of what he's saying. But I think that the witness can understand and follow and explain to us what it's all about; however, we need to have it viewed completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filic, you saw this recording. At that time, did you go to Malisevo; and if so, with who?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the anti-terrorist action took place on the road leading to Malisevo, foreign journalists and crews that were present in Pristina asked the head of the media centre that was located in the Grand Hotel, where they were too, to be given the possibility to go to Malisevo because their information was that everything had been razed to the ground, scorched, and so on. Of course, according to the procedure that I applied before that, I organized their trip to Malisevo, I took them on the very next day after the anti-terrorist action. This footage shows that the delegation of politicians, the leadership of the municipality of Malisevo is touring Malisevo and trying to make sure that normal conditions are ensured in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did we hear here a call to all the citizens of Malisevo to go back to their homes?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was this call to all the residents of Malisevo, saying that they would be safe because there is traffic now on the road leading to Orahovac, and for them it is of vital importance. It goes to Prizren too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is a reference made to aid and food, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is a reference to that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please be careful about the leading nature of these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Especially bearing in mind -- yes, I understand that, but it's really the witness that should be telling us from his own recollection of events. It's sufficient prompting. He's seen the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Filic, Malisevo that you toured at that time, was it razed to the ground?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: It was not razed to the ground. There weren't any damaged buildings at all in Malisevo because the terrorists had positions before Malisevo, and that is where -- from where they had blocked Malisevo. Malisevo, as a settlement, had not been damaged at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in spite of that some people reported to the effect that Malisevo had been razed to the ground?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: There probably were such reports by such agencies; however, as for the people who I took to Malisevo, they saw what the actual situation was. If they sent footage to the world, they could not provide false reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to show you the second part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have a date for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember roughly what the time was when this happened?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FILIC
utterances.text: I think that this was on the 28th or 29th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to play the video-clip from Junik for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, just one sentence in relation to the video-clip we saw before. Andrija Milosavljevic one of the Sainovic Defence witnesses, he testified about the previous video-clip and he confirmed its authenticity and his presence. 5D1239 is the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's your point, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to be of assistance to the Court so that you would have some additional facts made available to you, if necessary. That's all I wanted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can assure you all the previous evidence has been carefully logged and is coordinated on a regular basis. Just because I can't remember word for word all that's happened in this court in the past 21 months or so doesn't mean to say it's not all stored carefully in a way which will correlate it all in due course. So, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we instruct, Your Honour, the translators now to maybe try to translate this footage from Junik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may prove impossible because of the pace. What should happen in these situations is that there should be a transcript from which they can read, so that they can actually keep up with the pace of the translation. You've asked, you've made your request and we'll see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I kindly ask the translators to try to translate in English, please. [Interpretation] Can we play it now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, translation of that would have been impossible in the context of playing it that way. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon, Your Honour. Perhaps I am disturbing you, but when Veljko Odalovic testified, we played this video-clip and I believe that we provided part of what was said on paper. So the interpreters had the opportunity to use that then, so I will do my best to look it up and to provide the Trial Chamber with copies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now that you've directed our attention to it, Mr. Cepic, we will be able to find a copy of that without any difficulty. Mr. Lukic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to my colleague, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filic, tell us briefly, what was it that we saw in this footage? What was reported? What did you say? Could you please explain this for us a bit.
